speaker: A
text: Can an AI agent turn one sentence into a finished video?

speaker: B
text: It can help. The useful part is the production process. Here is how we use Framewright to keep that process organised.

speaker: A
text: What happens before anyone starts rendering?

speaker: B
text: We turn the idea into a brief: the audience, format, length, available material, and the job of each scene.

speaker: A
text: Does it just pick the newest tool?

speaker: B
text: It checks tools against the task and recorded tests. For this dog story, we combined an animated model, a three-dimensional forest, camera moves, and timed sound.

speaker: A
text: Could a game become material for a video?

speaker: B
text: Yes. Our Jekyll and Hyde game became a filming location for a book promo. The game supplied footage for another creative project.

speaker: B
text: Each scene connects what we say, what we show, the source material, and anything still missing. Measure the recorded speech, then build the timing around it.

speaker: A
text: If the exported file plays, are we done?

speaker: B
text: Not yet. Decode the export, inspect the pictures, and listen. Technical checks, creative approval, and publication are separate records.

speaker: A
text: What if a scene is too dark?

speaker: B
text: Keep the original. Make that section lighter, keeping the camera and timing. Compare the versions and record the result. We did exactly that with our manga-style city test.

speaker: B
text: The project keeps file versions, decisions, and open checks. We can reuse cleared material and prepare the video, thumbnail, captions, and publication text.

speaker: A
text: Give me one thing to try.

speaker: B
text: Pick one idea. Write three scenes: what you will say, what viewers will see, and where each asset comes from. That is your starting shot list.

speaker: A
text: Make the video. Keep the evidence.
